analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to tighten air-pollution limits on ethylene oxide, a cancer-causing industrial gas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its introduction and referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2019, no further action was taken before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a toxic industrial gas used mainly to sterilize medical equipment, and EPA's own scientists classified it as a human carcinogen. This bill ordered EPA to rewrite its emission limits for ethylene oxide using the agency's 2016 cancer-risk findings, apply the strongest available control technology to chamber exhaust vents at sterilization plants, and tell nearby residents within 30 days whenever a facility violates the new limits. If EPA failed to notify the public, its Inspector General would have to investigate. It was introduced by Rep. Brad Schneider with nine cosponsors from both parties and never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near ethylene oxide emitting facilities. The bill would have required stricter emission standards based on EPA's finding that the gas causes cancer, extra controls on exhaust vents, and prompt public notification of violations. In practice, that means residents of communities near sterilization plants, such as those in the Chicago suburbs the Illinois sponsors represent.

how_it_helps.text: Directs EPA to revise the ethylene oxide emission standards in federal regulations based on the results of the agency's December 2016 report evaluating the inhalation carcinogenicity of ethylene oxide.
Requires maximum achievable control technology — the strongest control standards used for hazardous air pollutant sources — to be applied to chamber exhaust vents at sterilization facilities.

Requires EPA to notify the public within 30 days of learning of a violation of the revised standards, and directs the EPA Inspector General to investigate any failure to notify, including the health risks caused by the failure.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that emit ethylene oxide — primarily chemical producers and commercial sterilization facilities — which would face new equipment and compliance costs, and potentially their customers if those costs are passed along.

drawbacks.text: Ethylene oxide is used to sterilize a large share of the nation's medical devices and supplies, so tighter emission rules raise compliance costs and could force plants to install expensive control equipment, relocate, or close.

The bill dictates a regulatory outcome by statute — mandating that EPA revise standards on a 180-day timeline based on one specific report — rather than letting the agency go through its normal rulemaking process, which is a fair objection from those who think agency scientists and cost-benefit analysis should set such standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes for nearby residents are large — EPA's own 2016 report found ethylene oxide far more carcinogenic than previously assumed — and the bill's costs fall on a specific industry with the technical means to control its emissions. The strongest honest objection is the bill's blunt, deadline-driven approach and the potential strain on the medical sterilization supply chain, but the public health benefit would have been substantial in affected communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Schneider introduced the bill on February 12, 2019, joined by four other Illinois Democrats as original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

Nine cosponsors — 8 Democrats and 1 Republican — signed on, but the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and no further action appears in the record after introductory remarks on February 26, 2019.
No version of the bill ever reached the House floor, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sterilization facilities and ethylene oxide emitting companies are better off because the bill died: no stricter emission standards, no mandated control technology for exhaust vents, and no 30-day public notification requirement for violations. Residents near those facilities got no new protections.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 12, 2019 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the record shows no committee action through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's ten supporters included 9 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the opposition was passive rather than partisan: the committee simply never acted on it.

industries.note: These plants use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices and would have faced stricter emission limits, mandatory control technology on exhaust vents, and public notification of violations. Their emissions are the direct health hazard the bill targets for the people living nearby.
Chemical manufacturers of the gas would face reduced demand flexibility as their customers absorb new compliance costs and equipment requirements.
They rely on ethylene oxide sterilization for a large share of medical products, so tighter rules could raise costs or disrupt supply, but many devices cannot be sterilized any other way.
